title: Violence Against Persons Prohibition Act (VAPP Act)

headings.title: Introduction and Historical Background of the VAPP Act
headings.content: The Violence Against Persons Prohibition (VAPP) Act is a landmark piece of legislation in Nigeria, signed into law in May 2015. Prior to the enactment of the federal VAPP Act, legal protections against domestic violence and gender-based violence (GBV) were fragmented, largely relying on the outdated Nigerian Criminal Code and Penal Code, which did not adequately address modern forms of abuse, marital rape, or harmful traditional practices. Civil society organizations, women's rights advocates, and legal professionals mounted sustained advocacy campaigns to push for a comprehensive legal framework that would criminalize all forms of violence and provide robust remedies for victims. Although initially enacted for the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Abuja, the VAPP Act serves as a model law meant to be domesticated by the various state houses of assembly across Nigeria's 36 states. Its introduction marked a paradigm shift from treating domestic violence as a private family matter to recognizing it as a serious criminal offense against the state. For nursing students and healthcare professionals in Nigeria, understanding this historical context is crucial, as it provides the legal backing necessary for identifying, managing, and reporting cases of abuse encountered daily in clinical practice.

headings.title: Core Objectives and Scope of the Legislation
headings.content: The primary objective of the VAPP Act is to eliminate all forms of violence against persons in private and public life, and to provide maximum protection and effective remedies for victims and punishment for offenders. Unlike previous legislation, the scope of the VAPP Act is expansive, covering various manifestations of abuse that disproportionately affect women, children, and vulnerable groups, though it is gender-neutral and protects men as well. The legislation seeks to address systemic gaps by ensuring that law enforcement agencies, the judiciary, and healthcare institutions work collaboratively to protect survivors. Its scope encompasses not only urban settings but also mandates awareness creation in rural areas where harmful traditional practices are deeply entrenched. For Nigerian nurses, the scope of this legislation directly impacts clinical protocols, requiring healthcare facilities to maintain accurate documentation, offer non-judgmental care, and facilitate prompt referrals to social welfare and legal aid services. By understanding the core objectives, healthcare providers become active participants in upholding human rights and enforcing protective measures within the Nigerian healthcare delivery system.

headings.title: Definitions and Categorization of Offenses
headings.content: The VAPP Act categorizes offenses into clear, legally actionable definitions to ensure perpetrators cannot exploit legal loopholes. These categories include physical violence, psychological and emotional abuse, sexual violence, harmful traditional practices, and economic abuse. Each category carries specific legal criteria that differentiate minor assaults from severe felonies. For instance, economic abuse involves the deprivation of economic or financial resources to which a person is entitled under the law, such as withholding household upkeep or denying access to employment. Psychological violence encompasses acts or omissions that cause mental or emotional suffering, including intimidation, harassment, or stalking. By clearly defining these offenses, the Act empowers healthcare professionals, social workers, and police officers to accurately identify the specific type of abuse a patient has experienced. Nurses must be familiar with these classifications because accurate patient history-taking and medical documentation serve as vital evidence in courts of law when prosecuting offenders under the VAPP Act.

headings.title: Physical, Psychological, and Emotional Violence Provisions
headings.content: Physical, psychological, and emotional violence provisions under the VAPP Act address some of the most pervasive forms of abuse encountered in domestic settings. Physical violence includes any act of physical force that causes pain, injury, or impairment, ranging from slaps and burns to severe beatings. Psychological and emotional violence, though lacking physical marks, inflicts profound trauma; it includes verbal abuse, constant humiliation, threats of harm, and isolation from family and friends. The Act recognizes that psychological abuse often precedes or accompanies physical violence and leaves lasting mental scars. In clinical practice, nurses frequently encounter patients presenting with psychosomatic symptoms, anxiety, depression, or unexplained physical injuries resulting from this spectrum of abuse. Healthcare providers must utilize trauma-informed care principles, offering a safe, empathetic environment where patients feel secure enough to disclose non-physical forms of abuse. Recognizing these provisions enables nurses to initiate multidisciplinary interventions involving psychiatric support, counseling, and protective social services.

headings.title: Sexual Violence and Harmful Traditional Practices
headings.content: Sexual violence and harmful traditional practices are heavily penalized under the VAPP Act due to their severe violation of bodily autonomy and human rights. Sexual violence provisions explicitly criminalize rape, attempted rape, sexual assault, forced isolation, and marital rape—a critical inclusion given that previous Nigerian laws did not recognize non-consensual sexual intercourse within marriage as a crime. Furthermore, the Act outlaws harmful traditional practices that degrade the dignity of women and girls, including female genital mutilation (FGM), forced marriage, widowhood rites that involve degrading or inhuman treatment, and forceful abandonment. These practices have historically been justified by cultural norms, but the VAPP Act supersedes customary laws that promote human rights violations. Nurses working in rural and urban Nigerian communities must be vigilant in identifying victims of FGM, forced child marriages, and sexual assault. Healthcare providers play a pivotal role in providing urgent post-rape care, administering emergency contraception, offering prophylaxis against sexually transmitted infections, and reporting these mandatory offenses according to legal and institutional guidelines.

headings.title: Rights and Protections of Victims and Survivors
headings.content: The VAPP Act establishes comprehensive rights and protections for victims and survivors of violence, ensuring they are treated with dignity, respect, and confidentiality. Key protections include the right to receive immediate medical, psychological, and social assistance, as well as access to emergency shelter and legal aid. The Act places a heavy emphasis on safeguarding survivors from revictimization, stigmatization, and intimidation by perpetrators or law enforcement agents. It also empowers courts to issue Protection Orders, which legally prohibit the abuser from contacting, approaching, or harassing the survivor. For nursing professionals, understanding these rights is essential when advocating for vulnerable patients within hospital settings. Nurses must ensure patient confidentiality is strictly maintained, coordinate with social workers to secure safe housing or shelter placements, and empower survivors by informing them of their legal rights to protection and compensation under the law.

headings.title: Penalties, Sentencing, and Legal Enforcement
headings.content: Penalties, sentencing, and legal enforcement mechanisms under the VAPP Act are designed to deter offenders and ensure justice through stringent punitive measures. Depending on the severity of the offense, penalties range from specified monetary fines to lengthy prison sentences without the option of a fine, particularly for heinous crimes like rape and trafficking. For example, aggravated rape carries mandatory minimum prison sentences, and repeat offenders face even harsher punitive measures. The Act also makes provisions for convicts to pay financial compensation and restitution to the victims for medical expenses incurred or property destroyed. Legal enforcement relies on active collaboration between law enforcement agencies, the judiciary, and medical personnel who supply forensic evidence. Nurses must understand these legal consequences so they can properly handle forensic evidence—such as clothing, bodily swabs, and physical injury charts—ensuring the chain of custody is unbroken so that perpetrators cannot escape justice due to technicalities during prosecution.

headings.title: The Role of Nurses and Healthcare Providers in VAPP Act Implementation
headings.content: Nurses and healthcare providers occupy a frontline position in the successful implementation of the VAPP Act. As trusted members of the community, nurses are frequently the first point of contact for survivors seeking medical attention for physical injuries, trauma, or reproductive health complications resulting from abuse. Consequently, healthcare professionals have a dual responsibility: to provide holistic, empathetic, and trauma-informed clinical care, and to meticulously document findings for legal documentation. Nurses must be trained to recognize subtle red flags of abuse, conduct non-threatening forensic examinations, and collaborate with multidisciplinary teams including social workers, psychologists, and legal aid officers. Furthermore, nurses play a vital advocacy role in educating communities about the provisions of the VAPP Act, debunking harmful myths, and dismantling cultural normalization of violence. By bridging the gap between healthcare and the legal justice system, Nigerian nurses become powerful agents of social change, ensuring that survivors receive both healing and justice.
